title: Generics preserve relationships
summary: Write a generic helper that returns the first item or null without unsafe casts.

scenario.briefing: A campus API returns lists of different types. Write one typed helper that preserves the element type.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.

hints: The return type already permits null.
The first item is items[0], which may be undefined.
Use the nullish coalescing operator to supply null.

misconceptions.description: Using as T to silence the empty-array case.
misconceptions.feedback: A cast does not add a value. Use ?? null to represent absence honestly.

misconceptions.description: Falling back to any when a generic gets difficult.
misconceptions.feedback: any disables the relationship you are trying to preserve. Use a type parameter or a constrained generic.

sections.title: TypeScript values and decisions
sections.body: TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript: const count: number = 3;. A union such as string | number keeps both alternatives visible until a runtime check narrows it. typeof, equality, and property checks narrow a union inside a branch. Arrays and loops keep their element types, so a transform returns a typed result.

sections.title: TypeScript source files
sections.body: The compiler erases types and emits JavaScript. The emitted code is what runs in the browser or Node.

steps.title: Generics and type safety

statements.label: A generic function can preserve the element type of its input.
A type assertion validates the runtime value.
T | null documents that absence is possible.
Using any is the safest way to generalize a helper.

steps.explanation: Generics carry the element type from input to output. A cast only tells the compiler to trust the author; it does not check the value.
